topic_bank.demand: Consider the average adult living in a wealthy country today. Would adopting a fully vegan diet (no meat, fish, dairy, or eggs) be, on balance, a better choice for that person than continuing a typical omnivorous diet? 'Better on balance' means weighing everything you consider relevant. Answer YES if you judge it would be better on balance; answer NO otherwise.
topic_bank.truth_conditions: modal: 'would be better' = better on balance for the person, NOT obligatory and NOT merely permissible; scope: the average adult in a wealthy country, present day; comparison: fully vegan diet (no meat, fish, dairy, eggs) versus continuing a typical omnivorous diet; threshold: YES iff better on balance, NO otherwise; no permanence clause (no 'forever/never again'); no added considerations.

topic_bank.demand: Consider wealthy countries today. Would raising their annual immigration admissions substantially — on the order of fifty percent or more above current levels — be, on balance, a better policy than keeping admissions near current levels? Answer YES if you judge the increase would be better on balance; answer NO otherwise.
topic_bank.truth_conditions: modal: 'better policy' = better on balance, NOT obligatory; scope: wealthy countries generally, present day; comparison: admissions raised ~50%+ versus admissions near current levels; threshold: YES iff the increase is better on balance, NO otherwise; no added considerations.

topic_bank.demand: Consider cities today. Is it, on balance, good policy for cities to have the option of charging drivers a fee to enter designated downtown zones during peak hours? The question is whether this option being available to cities is better on balance than it not being available — not whether every city should use it. Answer YES if you judge the option being available is better on balance; answer NO otherwise.
topic_bank.truth_conditions: modal: 'good policy' = better on balance; scope: cities in general, present day; comparison: the congestion-charging option being available to cities versus not available; threshold: YES iff availability is better on balance, NO otherwise; NOT asking whether every city should adopt it; no added considerations.

topic_bank.demand: Consider the modern job-seeking process as a whole — mass applications, multi-round interviews, and professional recruiters. Does this process consume substantially more economic resources (time, effort, money) than the value it produces? 'Substantially more' means the waste exceeds the value produced by a large margin, not merely that some waste exists. Answer YES if you judge the resources consumed substantially exceed the value produced; answer NO otherwise.

role_bank.register_notes: Speaks only within a ~850-word core English vocabulary (Ogden Basic English). Simple words for things, acts, and qualities; no technical, Latinate, or abstract policy terms. Ideas beyond the vocabulary get rebuilt from simple words or left unsaid. Short sentences, common connectives (and, but, if, because).

Types like a teenager texting: lowercase, abbreviations (idk, ngl, fr, tbh), emoji-adjacent particles (lol, lmao), no subordinate clauses, fragments over sentences. Emphasis by repetition ('so so bad') not adverbs. Uncertainty expressed as vibes ('idk lol') never as epistemic qualifiers. Anything formal reads as cringe and gets avoided.

Terse, concrete, land- and gear-focused speech. Short declaratives, rarely more than one clause. Understatement as default ('maybe' means no). Big ideas restated as what a man can see, do, or pack out. Statistical and policy vocabulary absent; dry humor present.

Writes like an effective-altruism forum regular: epistemic-status disclaimers, explicit probabilities ('~70% confident'), expected-value framing, QALYs, counterfactuals, steelmanning, numbered considerations. Hedging is saturated and precise; abstraction unlimited; jargon of rationality culture throughout.

Writes like a contracts attorney drafting an instrument: defined terms ('the Party', 'hereinafter'), nominalizations, enumerated clauses, provisos ('provided, however'), shall/may distinctions. Categorical rather than probabilistic; ambiguity is a defect; no colloquialisms; precision through structure rather than hedging.

Cadenced pulpit speech: repetition for rhythm ('I say to you, I say'), direct address ('brothers and sisters'), scriptural allusion, moral vocabulary rich (righteous, wicked, redemption), call-and-response markers ('can I get an amen'). Statistical and technical vocabulary absent; certainty is the register's default mode.
